name: blake3 (BLAKE3 hash)
baseline: SHA-256 (OpenSSL in the published chart); the Rust default is the sha2 crate, which uses SHA-NI or ARMv8 SHA2 instructions when the CPU has them
verdict_reason: The chart's 14x lead (6866 vs 484 MiB/s at 16 KiB) was measured with AVX-512 BLAKE3 against SHA-256 on a Cascade Lake CPU without SHA extensions. On a CPU with SHA extensions, a third party measured BLAKE3 almost 20% slower than SHA-256 at 1000 bytes and only twice as fast at 100,000 bytes. BLAKE3 still wins clearly on large inputs, on CPUs without SHA-NI, and with multiple threads.
tier_reason: Benchmark code, the hardcoded results, the machine (AWS c5.metal, Cascade Lake-SP 8275CL) and the flags are published in BLAKE3-specs.
claimed_speedup: 16 KiB input, 1 thread: 6866 MiB/s vs 484 MiB/s for SHA-256 (14x, derived from page data). Third party on a Ryzen 9 3900X with SHA extensions: BLAKE3 almost 20% slower than SHA-256 at 1000 bytes, twice as fast at 100,000 bytes.
workload: Single-threaded hashing of 16 KiB inputs (cargo bench '16384$'); third-party run: inputs of 4 bytes to 100,000 bytes.
hardware: AWS c5.metal, Intel Cascade Lake-SP 8275CL (AVX-512, no SHA extensions)
toolchain: BLAKE2 rows built with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native"; rustc version not stated
license: CC0-1.0 OR Apache-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
platforms: x86/x86_64 (SSE2 to AVX-512, runtime detection), aarch64 NEON, WASM; portable fallback; optional multithreading via rayon
one_liner: BLAKE3 hash: 14x SHA-256 on a 2019 AVX-512 server without SHA-NI, but slower than hardware SHA-256 on short inputs.
how_it_is_fast: BLAKE3 is a Merkle tree of 1 KiB chunks over a reduced-round BLAKE2s compression function, so independent chunks hash in parallel across SIMD lanes (up to 16 with AVX-512) and, with the rayon feature, across threads. Short inputs fill only one chunk and cannot use that parallelism, which is where hardware SHA-256 catches up.
use_it_when: Hashing large files or buffers, especially with the rayon feature
CPUs without SHA extensions (Intel client chips before Ice Lake, the Cascade Lake used in the chart)
You want a keyed hash, KDF, XOF and verified streaming from one algorithm
skip_it_when: Interoperability requires SHA-256 (TLS, certificates, Git, most protocols)
Messages around 1 KB or shorter on CPUs with SHA-NI or ARMv8 SHA2, where SHA-256 can be faster
Password hashing: BLAKE3 is fast by design
caveats: The chart's SHA-256 is OpenSSL, not the sha2 crate
Cascade Lake has AVX-512, which suits BLAKE3, and lacks SHA extensions, which hurts SHA-256, as the BLAKE3 author notes
The SHA-NI comparison used .NET's SHA256 on a Ryzen 9 3900X, not the sha2 crate
tradeoffs: Different digest from SHA-256: not a drop-in where hashes are stored or exchanged
The rayon feature adds a thread-pool dependency
